what: Archrock rents natural gas compression equipment and the people who run it. Its compressors push gas through gathering systems and pipelines, mainly in the Permian Basin and other US shale fields, under multi-year contracts. It also sells aftermarket parts and maintenance services for compressors that customers own themselves.
customers: Oil and gas producers and midstream pipeline companies in US shale basins, above all in the Permian, which need gas compressed to move it from wellhead to processing plant.
money: Fee-based rental of large horsepower compression units, with Archrock staff operating and maintaining them.
Parts, overhauls and maintenance for customer-owned compressors.
moat: Large compression units cost millions each and take months to build, so producers prefer to rent and let a specialist carry the capital and maintenance. Archrock’s fleet is one of the largest in the US, its contracts run for years and units stay on site for a long time, so customers rarely switch. Running near full utilisation gives it pricing power, and the 2024 and 2025 acquisitions of TOPS and NGCS added scale in the Permian.
risks: Debt of $2.35B against almost no cash means the balance sheet depends on steady cash flow.
Free cash flow is thin relative to earnings because new compressor purchases absorb most of operating cash flow, $502M of capex in 2025.
A sustained fall in gas or oil prices would slow drilling and eventually demand for new units.
Pricing has risen strongly in recent years and could flatten once compressor supply catches up.
Customer concentration in the Permian ties results to one basin’s infrastructure.
opportunities: Revenue nearly doubled from $781M in 2021 to $1.49B in 2025, while net income rose from $28M to $322M.
Natural gas demand from LNG export terminals and power generation for data centres keeps compression in short supply.
The shares trade at about 14 times earnings and 7.9 times EV/EBITDA with a 3.6% dividend yield.
Once growth capex slows, most operating cash flow of $720M a year could go to dividends, buybacks and debt reduction.
watch: Fleet utilisation and pricing per horsepower, growth capex plans for next year, leverage ratio, and dividend increases.
view: Archrock is a toll collector on American natural gas, and the toll has been going up. Compression is the unglamorous step between the well and the pipeline: gas has to be pressurised to move, the equipment is expensive and long-lived, and producers would rather rent it than own it. After a decade of low returns, the sector has become disciplined, utilisation is near full, and Archrock has been able to raise prices while adding scale through the TOPS and NGCS deals.

The earnings line tells that story clearly: net income went from $28M in 2021 to $322M in 2025 on revenue that doubled. Free cash flow looks modest at $120M for 2025 because the company is spending heavily on new units, but this is growth capex on contracts that are signed before the equipment is ordered. Treat the $720M of operating cash flow as the true earning power and the stock looks inexpensive at 7.9 times EV/EBITDA.

The investment turns on the length of the US gas build-out. LNG export capacity and gas-fired power for data centres argue for years of rising volumes from the Permian, which is where Archrock’s fleet sits. The main risk is leverage at $2.35B of debt if a commodity slump arrives while capex is high. At these prices I think the market is pricing a cyclical business, and the contract structure argues it deserves a steadier multiple.
bull: Gas volumes keep rising for LNG and power, compression stays tight and Archrock turns record operating cash flow into rising dividends and buybacks.
bear: A gas price collapse slows drilling just as new compressor supply arrives, squeezing pricing while debt is high.
